questions.q: What is "conditional formatting" in SSRS, mechanically?
options: An IIF or Switch expression set on a style property like Color or BackgroundColor
A dedicated Conditional Formatting dialog, separate from the Expression dialog
A rule you configure only on the Report Server, not in the report itself
A feature exclusive to charts, not text boxes or tables
questions.explain: There's no separate conditional-formatting feature — you set a style property (most often Color or BackgroundColor) to an expression, usually built with IIF or Switch.

questions.q: In =IIF(RowNumber(Nothing) MOD 2, Parameters!RowColor.Value, "White"), what does RowNumber(Nothing) do?
options: Returns the row number, counting from the outermost data region
Returns the total number of rows in the report
Returns Nothing (null) always
Returns the current page number
questions.explain: RowNumber(Nothing) counts rows starting at the outermost data region; the Nothing scope means renumbering begins at the first row of that region.

questions.q: What does MOD 2 accomplish in that same banding expression?
options: Returns 1 for odd row numbers and 0 for even ones, which IIF treats as true/false
Divides the row number by 2 and rounds to the nearest integer
Multiplies the row number by 2
Converts the row number to a string
questions.explain: MOD returns the remainder after division; row MOD 2 is 1 (truthy) for odd rows and 0 (falsy) for even ones, which is exactly what IIF needs to alternate colors.

questions.q: According to Microsoft's own expression reference, what expression turns a Color property red when Profit is negative?
options: =IIF(Fields!Profit.Value < 0, "Red", "Black")
=Fields!Profit.Value.Color
=Switch(Fields!Profit.Value, "Red")
=Format(Fields!Profit.Value, "Red")
questions.explain: This exact expression appears in Microsoft's expression-examples reference for the Color property: red for negative values, black otherwise.

questions.q: Where do the color name strings like "Red" or "PaleGreen" used in these expressions come from?
options: The .NET Framework's KnownColor enumeration
A custom SSRS-only color list with no relation to .NET
They must be hex codes, never names
They're defined per-report in a separate color palette file
questions.explain: Available colors in these expressions come from the .NET Framework KnownColor enumeration, which is why plain names like "Red" and "PaleGreen" work as string literals.
